chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Haytham al-Ajali (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Zakaria al-Qattan said: Bakr ibn Abdullah ibn Habib narrated to us, saying: Tamim ibn Buhlool narrated to us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Abdullah ibn al-Fazl al-Hashemi, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ziyad ibn al-Mundhir, who said: A group of the elders narrated to me, on the authority of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, that he said:

Those who startled the Prophet’s she-camel upon his return from Tabuk were fourteen: Abul Sharur, Abul Davahi, Abul Ma'azif, and his father, Talha, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Ubaydah, Abul A'war, al-Mughirah, Salim - the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah, Khalid ibn al-Walid, Amr ibn al-As, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. They are the ones about whom God, the Exalted, revealed: '…and they meditated a plot which they were unable to carry out.'

key_terms.تَبُوك: Tabuk, a location in northern Arabia where the Battle of Tabuk took place.
key_terms.مَوْلَى: Freedman or client (a non-Arab convert under the patronage of an Arab companion).
key_terms.وَهَمُّوا بِمَا لَمْ يَنَالُوا: And they meditated a plot which they were unable to carry out (Quranic quote).

ai.seo_question: Who were the fourteen companions mentioned in the hadith who startled the Prophet's camel and are linked to the Quranic verse 'wa hammū bimā lam yanālū'?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq cites this chain to identify fourteen companions, including prominent figures like Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-As, who were noted for their distinct negative traits or specific actions during the Prophet's return from Tabuk. The narration links them to the Quranic verse 'wa hammū bimā lam yanālū' (9:48), interpreting it as their internal plotting or failure to achieve their desired outcome against the Prophet, a theme often discussed in Shia exegetical traditions regarding the Ahl al-Suffah or specific companions depending on the context of the verse.
